paper_title: OWE-Bench: A long-horizon benchmark for measuring real-world engineering

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We present OWE-Bench (OpenWorldEngineer-Bench), a benchmark of 26 long-horizon engineering tasks written by domain experts in software engineering, physical engineering, machine learning, and scientific computing. Tasks range from optimizing kernels and designing an aircraft, to identifying the faults responsible for an earthquake. Each task requires significant domain knowledge and engineering work, with models averaging hundreds of millions of tokens per task. Solutions are scored on practical measures such as speed, cost and accuracy, both on provided cases the agent could test against and on hidden cases that an engineer would expect from the task description. The best-performing frontier model so far, Claude Fable 5.2, scores 54.6% and averages 211 million tokens per task. We highlight two findings. First, when models are given more time, they use more test-time compute and achieve higher scores. Models also scale differently with test-time compute: GPT-6 Astra achieves higher scores at shorter time limits and at equal token use, while Claude Fable 5.2 uses more tokens at longer limits to achieve the highest overall score. Second, each model scores lower on hidden cases than on the provided cases, by an average of 18 points, which we call the deployment gap. Models also fail to predict the deployment gap, overestimating their performance on hidden test cases by an average of 21 points. We hope that OWE-Bench grounds progress toward agents whose engineering solutions perform as well in deployment as they do in testing.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Frontier AI agents can now carry out substantial engineering work end to end [1, 2, 3, 4]. Given bug report, an optimization target or design goal, an agent can plan an approach, implement it, test it and revise its solution without step-by-step human direction. Prior to deployment, human is still expected to decide whether the agents work is ready to use. For agents to assume greater responsibility, they must be able to make this judgment themselves. Much of the difficulty in real engineering stems from the fact that goal can be clearly stated while also leaving certain decisions up for judgment. Those decisions include which conditions solution must handle and how much evidence is enough to show it is ready. An engineer must decide what to test, whether observed improvements will hold beyond those tests, which version to deliver, and whether further work is worth its cost. We ask: can agents tell when the job is done? Evaluating this ability requires distinguishing what an agent can establish during development from how its solution ultimately performs. final score measures the latter, but does not by itself reveal how reliable the evidence available to the agent was. Existing benchmarks evaluate agents on extended workflows, including repository changes, research engineering, model training and paper replication [5, 6, 7, 8, 9], but primarily report the quality of the final artifact. In SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench, hidden pass/fail tests determine success for the evaluator, but do not measure whether the agent could anticipate that outcome before submission. Other engineering benchmarks allow agents to query the graders own simulation while they work [10, 11], enabling them to optimize directly against it. Separating development from evaluation is basic principle of machine learning [12], yet agent benchmarks do not always enforce it [13], and when an agent can repeatedly query its final grader, generalization is hard to tell apart from optimization against the benchmark itself [14, 15]. Where final cases are hidden, as in MLE-bench and ALEBench [8, 16], benchmarks report how well the final work scores, but not how much of the improvement an agent measured during development survives on conditions it did not see. We built OWE-Bench to study engineering agents when the evidence available during development does not fully reveal how It contains 26 experttheir work will perform. Each task has continuous performance objective without predefined threshold for completion. Agents can develop, test and revise solutions using the evidence and tools available in their environments, but their final work is evaluated independently on hidden conditions they cannot inspect or query. Where the provided cases can be scored, we apply the same scoring rule to provided and hidden cases to measure the deployment gap: the difference between performance demonstrated during development and performance on unseen conditions. We call this setting open-world because agents must decide what to test, which solution to deliver, and when to stop without observing all the conditions that determine final performance. We release the benchmark and agent trajectories alongside the leaderboard. We review related work in Section G. Our contributions are: 1. long-horizon benchmark for engineering autonomy. OWE-Bench comprises 26 expertauthored tasks, requiring hundreds of millions of tokens to solve, with continuous objectives and independent evaluation on hidden conditions, designed to leave consequential engineering decisions to the agent (Sections 2 to 4). We establish leaderboard across fourteen frontier models (Section 5). 2. measurement of the deployment gap. By comparing performance on development and hidden cases, and collecting agents own forecasts, we show that development evidence helps identify stronger solutions but substantially overstates their performance on unseen conditions (Section 6). 3. study of how agents use their time. Running six models at varying time limits, we show that every model scores higher with more time, but that models differ in how much of limit they use and how much more time helps them, so the order of the models changes with the limit. Surprisingly, even when an agent never runs out of time, the amount of time it is given can change how well it performs (Section 7).

sections.title: 2 Design Principles
sections.content: Three principles govern what agents can use, how their solutions are scored, and when they stop. Information boundary. Each task gives the agent starting solution, documentation, and data, examples or tests to guide development. The final solution is scored on held-out cases or operating conditions. These may follow the development distribution or differ from it to test transfer [17]. At submission, we freeze only the declared artifact paths. An isolated offline verifier evaluates them with pristine task-supplied checking code where applicable; packages installed during development do not carry over. Scores come from execution, geometric comparison or simulation, never from an LLM judge, whose verdicts can favor their own outputs [18, 19], miss code errors [20] and be swayed by inserted text [21, 22]. No pass mark. solution can pass correctness checks and still have room to improve. Tasks therefore use continuous scores on measures such as speed, cost, geometric error and forecast skill. Each task defines floor for missing, invalid or rulebreaking submissions, baseline for the starting 3 Agent environment Baseline artifact Provided cases Implement Evaluate Revise Candidate versions v2 v3 v4 1 Selection Time used stop stated budget 3 Stopping Sealed evaluation Frozen submission Isolated verifier Development score Hidden score OWEBench below the best-known design; eight come from model or reference solution of what is attainable, as for most forecasting tasks; and two are targets set by the task authors. Some ceilings may be out of reach, while others may be exceeded. Normalized scores therefore compare remaining room for improvement only roughly and are not percentages of human capability. There is no pass mark that tells the agent its work is finished. The agent must make that judgment, which we test in Section 7. Open book, fixed toolbox. Agents may use public methods, but must build with the tools and files already in the environment. They can search and read pages from web snapshot dated 1 October 2026 [25], but cannot download packages, code, data or models. Tasks are accepted only when adapting public work leaves substantial engineering (Section 3.2). The shared snapshot and tools standardize access across evaluation dates, but do not control prior knowledge or search rankings (Section C.2).

Eight tasks ask agents to make existing software faster or smaller while preserving required functionality. Examples include OxiLite, SPARQL store on SQLite [28, 29], Parquet lakehouse [30], an exactly-once streaming pipeline under fault injection, and the MicroPython VM and LVGL renderer on an RV32 guest [31, 32, 33]. Models and kernels. Machine learning tasks ask agents to post-train or extend small language models within compute budget, such as teaching Qwen3-8B [34] chess tactics or extending SmolLM2 [35] from 8k to 64k context. These tasks ask agents to implement GPU kernels for quantum-chemistry integrals [38] and seismic wave propagation, fill cloud gaps in Sentinel-2 time series [39], and relocate an earthquake sequence. Other tasks use past records to forecast pollutant plumes, storm surge and reaction kinetics under new conditions. Forecasts and reconstructions are scored against held-out observations or ground truth. Physical engineering: CAD reconstruction. sections.title: 3.2 Task difficulty and remaining headroom
sections.content: We assess task difficulty using three sources of evidence: the performance of existing public methods, the targets used to define task ceilings, and the gains from giving agents more time to complete the work. Public methods fall short of task targets. Where applicable, authors ran the closest public tools end to end, including EPA AERMOD for plume dispersion [40], VELEST and hypoDD for earthquake relocation [41, 42, 43], and ANUGA for storm surge [44]. None of the tested methods scored above 0.259 against ceiling of 1 (task versions differ from the leaderboard), so each task demands substantial engineering beyond the best public starting point. Ceilings estimate achievable performance. Targets are exact answers, engineering bounds or estimates of attainable performance, so improving on known implementation need not saturate task (Section 2). Additional time leaves substantial headroom. Across five tasks, doubling the time from half the limit to the full limit raises Opuss and Sols scores by 10 points, yet their full-length runs still finish 50 points below the ceiling. On two of these tasks, one more hour in new run only adds half point (Section 7).

sections.title: 4 How the Tasks Were Built
sections.content: Experts. Tasks were built by domain experts recruited through Mercor who held masters or PhD in their field, had at least ten years of experience, or both. Before implementation, each expert proposed task identifying relevant public work, the engineering work that remains after adapting it, the required deliverable, and how its correctness and performance would be verified. Maintainers reviewed each proposal before the expert built the task. Review gates. Tasks were reviewed for grading correctness, resistance to exploits and difficulty. Isolated grading. The verifier runs separately from the agents workspace; build-time checks verify that missing or invalid submissions receive the score floor and that the unchanged starting solution receives the expected baseline score on the specified hardware. Red-team trials. The agent receives brief, working starting design, parts catalog and the autopilots code, but cannot run the simulator that grades it. For up to eight hours it iterates: measuring parts with budgeted bench tools, writing its own models of the physics, designing and checking the aircraft, and flying few practice flights. private simulator then flies the submitted aircraft in 34 hidden conditions. The aircraft shown is Claude Fable 5.2s best design, the only one of 112 attempts to reach the ceiling. out completing the intended engineering work, including when given access to the verifiers source code. Difficulty trials. Tasks were rejected in their current form when frontier agents mean score over three attempts reached two-thirds of the way from the baseline to the performance ceiling. Automated static checks and an LLM-assisted rubric review additionally assessed task structure, reproducibility, instructions, score design and time and compute budgets. Each task required approval from three human reviewers before acceptance. Roughly 400 tasks made it through automated checks, but only the 26 best were accepted to the benchmark. After evaluation, we audited every agent trajectory for unfair failures and attempted exploits (Section 8). The difficulty gate deliberately selects against tasks on which frontier agents already perform well. Low scores are therefore partly consequence of benchmark construction, as in other adversarially filtered evaluations [45, 46]. Our results characterize agents capabilities and limitations on this selected set of tasks, rather than their performance on typical engineering work. Difficulty filtering can also bias comparisons against models used to select tasks [47]. To mitigate this risk, we draw on Phang et al.s suggestion to use diverse adversary models, calibrating each tasks difficulty using GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, Opus 5.5, and Fable 5.1.

sections.title: 5.3 Token and cost efficiency
sections.content: Figure 14 compares performance with the tokens and model cost consumed per attempt [13, 67]. Claude Fable 5.2 has the highest mean while using 210.7 million tokens and $105.08 per attempt, and it lies on both frontiers. GPT-6 Astra averages 44.2% with 88.8 million tokens and $234.63; GPT-6.1 Sol averages 41.2% at $52.12, and Claude Sonnet 5.5 39.0% at $38.65. Astra uses fewer total tokens than Sol, Sonnet or Fable 5.2 but costs more, illustrating why token volume and dollar cost give different comparisons. Claude Fable 5.1 costs $87.70 per attempt for 29.1%: more than Sonnet, for lower score. Measured by tokens rather than time (Figure 1, left), GPT-6 Astra scores highest at every token count its runs reach, and Fable 5.2 pulls ahead only by using more tokens than Astra uses at any limit. By cost (right), GPT-6.1 Sol scores highest from its cheapest runs, about $0.33 per attempt, up to its full-limit cost of about $50, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash scores highest below that. An agent never sees the hidden evaluation cases, so how it judges its own work rests on its internal knowledge, provided examples, held-out splits of its own data or tests, and anything accessible on the web. This evidence serves two distinct purposes: determining which of its versions is better, and whether version will hold up in deployment. To measure both, we score each final artifact on its tasks provided cases with the same formula as the hidden grader, so every trial gets development score next to its hidden score. This is also the score that benchmark grading agents on the cases they could see would report. It measures the evidence an agent has to judge by, not the agents own judgment, and on some tasks, such as aircraft design, the agent cannot compute it directly. To measure the judgment itself, we asked each model to forecast the hidden and development scores of each of its runs from the runs log (Section B.7). We leave out the four forecasting tasks because their artifact is itself the forecast for the hidden cases, and the B300 attention engine because grading its development workloads would be too costly (Section B).

sections.title: 6.1 Agents can tell which of their versions is better
sections.content: Development scores tell an agent which of its attempts is likely to do better on the hidden cases. For each model and task, we pick one of the eight attempts by its development score, much as code generators pick among samples by running tests [70, 71], and compare its hidden score with that of random attempt and of the oracle, the attempt the hidden grader would pick in hindsight. Among eight attempts, picking by development score raises the hidden score by 6.4 points over random attempt (95% CI 5.1 to 7.6), about half of the oracles gain (Figure 8 and Table 2). Selecting based on development scores doesnt depend on any hidden scoring, so an agent can use it (unlike the oracle, which requires knowing the hidden scores). The gain is positive on 20 of the 21 tasks (its 95% interval is above zero on 13), does not hinge on any one model or 8 OWEBench task, and replicates on new attempts. It also holds on new cases that no agent saw: on fresh aircraft flights and concrete buildings, picking by development score still clearly beats random attempt (Section B.2). Ranked by development scores, the fourteen models also keep most of their hidden order (rank correlation 0.96). The agents own forecasts rank their attempts too: picking by forecast recovers 41% of the oracles gain, against 50% for the development score on the same attempts (Section B.7). Agents also make the same judgment within run, as they must choose which artifact they want graded (each submission is pinned commit, and the last one is graded). On average, the artifact the agent chooses to submit only falls short of the best artifact by under 2 points and picking among runs submissions by development score would gain less than point over the agents own choice. This suggests that agents are already effective at judging what their best work looks like (Section B.8).

Their development scores run 67 to 70 points high, and on bearing transfer every artifact scores perfectly on its development data, so the score cannot even rank attempts. Agents expected gap here, but of only 15 to 18 points, and forecast hidden scores of 75 to 82 against actual 24 to 33. On software tasks, hidden workloads catch failures that public ones miss, even where the two are drawn alike, as stronger test suites do for generated code [73, 74]. One software attempt in seven passes every development check yet scores zero on the hidden workloads. As result, selecting by development score recovers only third of the oracles gain, illustrating how false positives limit resampling with imperfect verifiers [75]. Where provided cases ship with their answers, scores run high but mostly keep their order: on drawing-to-CAD and parametric CAD, and on aircraft design, whose test flights differ by design, development scores run 13 to 19 points high, yet picking by them still recovers 66 to 83% of the oracles gain. The exception is one model whose development scores run far ahead of its hidden ones. Gemini 4 Argons development scores exceed its hidden ones by 35 points, about twice the median of the other thirteen models. Going only by development score would lift Argon from eighth to fifth (Figure 9), and its self-estimates of performance overshoot the most out of any model, by 40 points. Argon ranks first on the development parts of drawing-to-CAD and scan-to-CAD, and seventh and eighth on the hidden parts (Section B.4), and on the three CAD tasks its attempt with the best development score does no better than random one.

sections.title:
6.3 More checking does not close the gap: the
checks look like the cases agents have
sections.content: If agents misjudged their work because they did not check it, more checking would help. We examined this through pipeline inspection, check removal, and an experiment encouraging additional validation. We see that agents already perform many checks. An audit of all runs found the agents own estimate of its score in 89% of them. Similar to the agents post-run forecasts, these in-run estimates overstate hidden performance by 25 points. Even when agents knew their development scores, they overestimated hidden performance by 18.5 points, 9 about as much as the 20.4-point gap between development and hidden scores on those tasks. This suggests the checks agents build for themselves provide little more information than the provided cases do. Half the runs name risk that the work will not generalize, yet those runs forecasts overshoot as much as the rests (Section B.7). In six models final pipelines, 92% of drawingand scan-toCAD pipelines compare the solid they built with the input, as in visual self-verification for CAD code [76]. Yet pipelines that check have about the same gap as those that do not, Argon checks in 14 of 16 pipelines and has the largest gaps, and removing the checks from Sols pipelines lowers its development scores more than its hidden ones (Section B.12). Telling agents to validate does not help either. We gave finished full-length runs on the concrete and page layout tasks one more hour to work, with either neutral instruction or one to check each change against the current submission on the provided cases and keep the original if nothing validates as better. With the validation instruction, agents re-submitted their artifact unchanged about seven times as often (18% against 3%), yet scored no better (0.1 points, 95% CI 1.8 to 1.7; Section B.11). In nearly nine of ten continuations that ended worse than they started, the development score held or rose. These findings suggest that the limitation is not simply how often agents check their work, but what their checks cover. Where development scores misled, the failed attempts show agents failing to account for cases outside of those they were given (Section B.6). GPT-6.1 Sol sped up MicroPythons practice programs rather than the interpreter and judged its speed only on them and Argon added shortcuts to the SPARQL store that relied on quirks of the practice data. Additional checks against the same limited cases may reinforce apparent improvements without revealing failures under new conditions.

sections.title: 7 Can Agents Tell When to Stop?
sections.content: A time limit can constrain performance by ending run, but it can also influence how an agent plans and allocates effort before the limit is reached. Which of the two matters depends on the model. We ran six models at varying time limits, from 1/128 to 1/2 of each tasks limit, and compared them with their leaderboard runs at the full limit (Figure 1; Section B.10). The two GPT models work right up to the 10 OWEBench limit. GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol use essentially all of every limit and make use of background commands so they can keep working while waiting for results. The two Claude models stop on their own. Claude Fable 5.2 uses 82 to 88% of whatever limit it is given and Claude Opus 5.5 60 to 75%, across 128fold range. They start background jobs less often, and at the longer limits they spend about half their time waiting for commands to finish. They also submit about twice as many versions as the GPT models. Working to the limit pays when time is short: Astra leads Fable 5.2 by 5 to 7 points at every limit up to 1/8, and Fable 5.2 beats it on at most 4 of the 26 tasks at 1/16 and below. But the Claude models gain more as the limit grows. For the GPT models each doubling adds about the same, roughly 5 points, while for the Claude models the gain rises from about 2 points at the shortest limits to about 10 at the longest. Fable 5.2 draws level with Astra at quarter of the limit and leads by 10 points at the full one, and Opus trails both GPT models at every shorter limit but draws level with them at the full limit. GLM-5.3 uses most of each limit and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash even less as the limit grows, but each gains only about 11 points across the whole range. Because the Claude models consistently use set percentage of whatever limit they are allocated, it appears they plan their work around the provided constraints rather than the inherent demands of the task. We isolate this effect by varying Claude Opus 5.5s stated time budget while keeping the task and tools fixed. When told it had eight hours instead of four, Opus scored 14.3 points higher on aircraft design (95% CI 8.2 to 20.7) and 7.1 points higher on stormsurge forecasting (3.6 to 10.5),1 even though most of its eight-hour runs finished within four hours (38 and 40 of 48; Figure 10). Under the four-hour limit, Opus stopped sooner, often after roughly an hour on aircraft design, leaving most of its allotted time unused. No run reached its limit, so the only difference was the limit Opus was told. Opus reads its deadline early in run and paces its work to fit. Across the five tasks of the split test below, halving the leaderboards limit cost it 11 points, and on the aircraft task, raising the limit from eight hours to sixteen added another 10.8 (2.1 to 19.3). Other mod1 The main text uses normalized points, as on the leaderboard, except for the search study, which reports task reward. The tests were pre-registered on task reward, which Section B.9 reports; it gives the same conclusions. els behave differently. On the aircraft task, GLM5.3 worked the same hours and scored the same whether it was told it had eight hours or sixteen (Section B.9). More time spent working does not always improve the final submission: on the aircraft task, some agents kept working past their best design and ended up submitting worse one (Section B.8). The stated time limit is therefore part of the evaluation condition, not merely cap on available compute. It can change performance without being reached and, because models respond to it differently, it can change the gaps between them. Because agents can tell which attempt is better (Section 6.1), one might trade time for attempts and let development scores choose. Stopping early costs more than choosing wins back. Earlier work found that the better split depends on the setting: in REBench some agents did best with many 30-minute attempts and others with fewer 2-hour ones [2], and on math problems the best mix of sequential and In parallel compute depends on difficulty [77]. randomized test on five tasks that span all four domains, Opus and Sol were run once with the full time limit or twice with half the limit each, submitting whichever scored better on the provided cases (Section B.9). Even picking the better one in hindsight loses by 3.4 points. On no task did two shorter runs beat one longer one. The margin follows what the lost time is worth: 13 points on model training, 7 to 8 on the building and aircraft designs, and tie on page layout and gap-filling, where half the time costs least. Returns do flatten toward the end of run: on the concrete and page layout tasks, the hidden score rises by about 9 points in the second quarter of full-length run and 2 in the last, and one more hour in new run adds half point (95% CI 1.0 to 2.0; Sections B.8 and B.11). Therefore, although the marginal gains from longer runs diminish, they remain more valuable than the additional selection opportunities created by splitting the budget.

sections.title: 8 Reward Hacking and Cheating
sections.content: An agent that cannot see how it will be graded may try to reach the grader instead. Long, open-ended runs give an agent many chances to game its grader 11 OWEBench [78, 79, 80, 81], so we checked every trial. Exploit attempts are rare, no attempt to tamper with the grader raised score, and no exploit changes models rank. We count trial as an exploit attempt when the agents commands show it pursuing the score without doing the intended engineering work, for example by altering evaluation machinery, recovering hidden answers or exploiting gaps between the task and its checks. LLM reviewers read every trial, and each counted finding was checked by hand (Section D). Across the fourteen models, 38 of 2,912 trials (1.3%) contain an attempt. Tampering with the grader never raised score, because the verifier uses its own pristine source tree and checking code; Inkling, for example, edited repositorys patch collector to hide changes outside the allowed paths. Attempts to recover hidden answers also failed: Sol brute-forced private generator seeds without finding them. Attempts that exploited the task itself earned little. Argons hard-coded fast paths for public MicroPython functions failed hidden checks, and parametric CAD programs that returned stored public models scored little above the tasks baseline, which is the score of such copy. Eight attempts earned nonzero reward; we set those scores to zero, which lowers no models mean by more than 0.13 points. Attempts are not confined to the weakest models: Argon, in the middle of the leaderboard, has the highest attempt rate, 5.3% (Section D.1).

sections.title: 9 Discussion
sections.content: Telling when the job is done. Our findings distinguish an agents ability to improve engineering work from its ability to judge when that work is complete. Agents often select their strongest submitted versions, but development performance can substantially overstate performance on unseen cases, the agents themselves expect far higher scores than they get, and stated deadlines can influence when agents stop even without being reached. Benchmarks with pass/fail grading measure whether submission meets set of criteria, while benchmarks with final grader allow agents to optimize directly against the specific evaluation conditions. Neither establishes how well an agent can judge its work without final evaluation feedback. Graded on the cases they could see, every model in our study would score higher, and the model that fit those cases most would gain most (Argon would rank fifth rather than eighth). Separating development from evaluation therefore changes both the level of an agent benchmarks results and, where an agent fits its provided cases, the ordering of models. What development evidence is good for. Running several attempts and submitting the one with the best development score recovers about half of the best-of-eight gain without hidden grade, and within run, agents already submit their best version most of the time; retrospectively selecting among their submissions offers little additional gain, while instructing agents to validate against existing provided cases does not improve hidden performance in our follow-up experiments. Choosing well does not replace time, though, because the limit shapes how much an agent does: in our randomized test, one long run beat two shorter ones on three of five tasks and tied on the other two, so time is better spent on longer runs than on more attempts. Development scores stop being guide where an agent has fit its provided cases, as Argon did on the CAD tasks and three software tasks. choice is only as trustworthy as the evidence the agent had no incentive to game. Why some agents fit their provided cases is open. One speculative explanation, which we have not tested for any model, is training that rewards passing the tests an agent can see. Developers have reported models learning to special-case or bypass unit tests during reinforcement learning on coding tasks [82, 79]. Instructions change agent behavior more than their scores, except the time limit. Instructing agents on how to work changed what the agents did, but not how well they scored. Told to research prior work, nearly every agent searched (Section C.3) and told to validate, agents held back their changes (Section 6.3). The time limit changed both: Opus did less and scored lower with half the limit, and did more and scored higher with twice the limit, without reaching either (Section 7). With no pass mark to stop at (Section 2), how much of the limit an agent uses is largely its own choice, and models differ in whether they plan around the limit at all: the Claude models stop at set share of whatever limit they are told, while the GPT models work right up to it (Section 7). benchmarks time limit is therefore part of its task: scores at one limit need not carry over to another, the order of the models changes with it (Figure 1), and time used belongs next to each score, as in Table 1. 12 OWEBench Access to published methods is not the bottleneck. Offering web search does not measurably change scores, even when nearly every agent searches. Five models ran every task with and without search over the snapshot, and search changed their mean task reward by +0.003 (95% CI [0.011, 0.018]). Under the default prompt only 13% of trials used it, so we also told Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol to research prior work before writing any code. On five tasks, 79 of 80 such trials searched, yet they scored the same as trials given the same instruction without web access (task reward difference 0.000, 95% CI [0.035, 0.035]). The trajectories offer possible explanation. Agents often name the relevant method before they search. Search mostly supplies facts about the local setup, such as an instructions syntax or librarys API, and ideas the same model reaches without it: 132 of the 180 retrieved ideas that reached final artifact also appear in that models offline runs. The hard part of these tasks is adapting known methods to the problem at hand, not finding them (Section C). Limitations. Tasks were accepted partly because agents struggled with them, so the scores describe this suite rather than research and engineering work in general. sections.title: 9.1 Release
sections.content: We release all tasks and evaluation trajectories with the leaderboard. Every task file and released trajectory carries canary string so that they can be filtered from training data [83], and evaluations with search must use snapshot dated before the tasks release, so that these materials cannot be retrieved [84].

sections.title: 10 Conclusion
sections.content: OWE-Bench asks whether agents can tell when the job is done: whether their work will hold up on cases they never saw, and when it is good enough to stop. Across 26 tasks, agents often submit their strongest versions, and development evidence helps select better solutions across independent attempts. But solution that performs well on the cases used to develop it may fail on new workloads, inputs or conditions. Across 21 tasks, final artifacts scored 18 points higher on provided cases than on unseen cases, and asked to forecast their scores on the unseen cases, agents overestimated them by 21 points. Additional validation against the same limited evidence did not reliably uncover these failures. Stated time limits also shaped when agents stopped, even when those limits were never reached. Together, these findings expose gap between improving an engineering solution and knowing whether it is ready to deliver. As agents take on greater responsibility for engineering work, the challenge is not only to improve the solutions they produce, but also their ability to judge what the available evidence establishes, what remains uncertain, and when further work is justified.

Twenty-one tasks are eligible, and Table 5 gives each ones class. The four forecasting tasks are not, because their artifact is fixed forecast or catalog for the hidden cases, and grading the B300 attention engine on its 48 development workloads takes about 1.5 B300-hours per artifact, so it was not run. Chesss development puzzles ship with their answers but are drawn like the hidden ones, so we class them by distribution. The pooled analyses cover all fourteen models; the follow-up tests below name the models they use. For each modeltask cell of eight attempts, three policies choose one attempt: random, the mean of the eight hidden scores; development selection, the hidden score of the attempt with the highest development score, with ties averaged; and the oracle, the highest hidden score. Selection uses the raw development reward, because normalization clipping can create ties that are not real. Some task rewards are also capped inside the tasks own formula. Page layouts reward is the worst startup familys mean page saving divided by 0.40, capped at 1, and bearingfault-transfers is clipped at target balanced accuracy; where an artifact reaches such cap on the provided cases, selection falls to the tie rule even if the uncapped objective still separates candidates. The primary endpoint is development selection minus random, pooled with tasks weighted equally and models equally within task, with task-stratified bootstrap interval and sign-flip permutation test. sections.title: Appendix C Web Search Study
sections.content: C.1 Setup Five models (Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol, Gemini 4 Argon and GLM-5.3) ran all 26 tasks with eight trials in each of two arms with identical budgets: search disabled, or search and page fetch over the 1 October 2026 snapshot. The arms share the system prompt and first message except for Web access section, which reads You have web search tool and page fetch tool. Use them whenever they would help with the task. or You do not have web access. Search returns up to ten results with short highlights, and fetch returns pages stored text from at or before the cutoff, with no live fallback. run may make 50 searches and 100 page requests. After each web result, the agents own model updates short research notes that survive context compaction; their cost counts toward the trial. In the follow-up, Opus and Sol were told on five tasks: Do your due diligence before you write any code: use the web search and page fetch tools to research the prior work on this problem (methods, papers, libraries, reference implementations), even if the task looks self-contained. Then reuse what fits rather than building from scratch. Matched controls received the same instruction, asking for research from what you know and what is already in the environment, without web access. C.2 Snapshot integrity The cutoff is set on every request and never shown to the agent, and the web tools run outside the agents sandbox, which has no network access. Tests of the snapshot service returned none of 1,100 objects created after their cutoffs. In content audit, 3 of 300 research-paper search sessions and 1 of 300 codelibrary sessions returned post-cutoff or undatable content. In forecasting check, model predicting 150 resolved Polymarket questions from snapshot results scored level with the market price at each questions cutoff, while with only publication-date filter, which lets later content through, it beat the market by 0.052 in Brier score. content cutoff does not reconstruct the search engines ranking at that date: matched-pair test found the snapshot slightly favoring papers and packages that became prominent after the cutoff, about as much as live search does [97, 25]. C.3 Results Each models score averages its eight trials per task with tasks weighted equally. The search effect is the difference between the arms, averaged over the five models, with intervals from hierarchical bootstrap over tasks and then trials [63]. Scores use common scoring, gap-halving-v1, and the grades of the 5 November analysis snapshot; later leaderboard corrections are not applied, because the Stateful Parquet layout check was run only on search-enabled trials. Few trials search under the default prompt, so this estimates the effect of offering search, not of using it [98]. Figure 11 gives each models estimate, and no single tasks difference survives correction for testing 26 tasks. The follow-ups matched controls ran two days after its search runs rather than interleaved with them. C.4 What search changed review of 363 web-using trials, blind to model and score, covered 135 from the five-model search study, 94 additional Grok trials, 55 research-prompt pilot trials and the 79 search-using follow-up trials. It coded each retrieval episode: whether it was already planned, whether offline runs contain the same idea, and whether it reached the final artifact. Retrieved content changed the final artifact in 110 trials (30%): 72 helped, 35 were unclear, 3 were neutral and none 30 OWEBench cutes such an action and the commands themselves show its purpose, for example editing collector, sweeping generators private seeds or returning stored public answers by part name. Stated reasoning can support count but is never needed for one, because models reveal very different amounts of it. Attempts later reverted or blocked count. Reusing public methods and code is allowed; ambiguous specification gaming [101], benchmark seeking and false claims of success are recorded separately. LLM reviewers read every trial, and each counted finding was checked by hand against the commands, instructions and grader. The released audit data list every deliberate exploit attempt found in the audited leaderboard runs, with recorded rewards. Eleven borderline cases, such as running development measurements through an edited copy of checker or briefly editing local build script, are not counted. They are listed with the released audit data, together with trial identifiers, step numbers and the items judged allowed. Instructed red-team trials from construction (Section 4) are not part of this audit. D.1 Observed attempts Observed strategies and defenses. Attempts ranged from simple gate evasion to coordinated tampering [102]. Beam renamed unchanged starter code to bypass submission gate; all four trials scored zero. Inkling edited repositorys index and patch collector to conceal changes outside the allowed paths, then reverted them. The verifier uses its own pristine source tree and checking code, and no observed grader-tampering attempt Sol tried to reconstruct hidden raised score. answers by brute-forcing private generator seeds; neither search succeeded. Searches for benchmark solutions, which elsewhere have found the answers to the benchmark being run [84, 103], also returned nothing through the web snapshot, which predates task release. Other attempts exploited the task itself. Argon hardcoded fast paths for public MicroPython functions in seven trials, which all failed hidden checks. On parametric CAD, Inkling, Kimi and Argon copied public worked-example geometry in ten trials, six of which earned some reward. The task asks for converter from unfamiliar drawings, but these programs instead returned stored public models, or templates cut from them, chosen by the part-family name in Figure 11. Search has no measurable average effect at low or near-universal uptake. Differences in task-weighted mean reward with 95% intervals; right-hand labels give the share of search-enabled trials that used web tool. Top: default prompt, all 26 tasks, with hierarchical bootstrap intervals; estimates include trials that never searched. Bottom: Opus and Sol told to research prior work, against controls with the same prompt and no web access, on five tasks, with intervals of 1.96 standard errors across tasks. hurt, though three other trials lost two hours or more to abandoned web-inspired branches. Of the 180 retrieved ideas that reached an artifact, 132 also appear in the same models offline runs. Facts about the local setup unblocked existing plans: an Opus B300 trial that had already planned tensor-core kernels looked up the exact instruction syntax and had faster passing kernel nine minutes later, and Sol trials on stateful-parquet retrieved missing DuckDB C-API signatures and had working bridge minutes later. Methods from other settings often did not fit: Sol B300 trial built an exp2 emulation that the installed code disables for this GPU, measured it 2 20% slower and abandoned it. These are annotations, not causal effects on scores.

This includes altering evaluation machinery, recovering hidden answers, or exploiting gaps between the task and its checks. We count trial as an exploit attempt only when the agent exe31 each request. The tasks baseline is the score of such copy, so these lookups earned little above it: three of the six normalize to zero and the other three to 3 to 21 points, before being set to zero. GLM and Grok also each kept scratch memory outside the tasks declared workspace in one B300 trial, so we set those two scores to zero. The released audit data record the attempts and their outcomes. D.2 Audit scope and score sensitivity OWEBench Every one of the 2,912 leaderboard trials was reviewed, 208 per model. Download attempts and benchmark seeking are reported separately from counted exploits. Moreover, all shell downloads failed and no benchmark search returned task material. Nevertheless, zero observed attempts does not establish absence of exploit behavior. Figure 12. Performance and exploit attempts. All fourteen models; labels give trials with attempts / total trials. Zero means none observed. Attempts by model. Across the fourteen models, 38 of 2,912 trials (1.3%) contain an identified attempt (Figure 12). sections.title: Appendix G Related Work
sections.content: evaluation. SWE-bench Long-horizon and Terminal-Bench evaluate agents in repositories and command-line environments [5, 6], and FrontierSWE gives agents up to 20 hours on performance engineering, scientific computing and ML research [4]. RE-Bench, MLE-bench, PaperBench and PostTrainBench extend evaluation to research engineering, model training and replication [2, 8, 9, 3]. SWE-Marathon gives agents 2 to 10 hours on software tasks that take experts 40 to 400 hours [7], KernelBench and SciCode target GPU kernels and research code [104, 105], and Kwa et al. [1] measure how the length of tasks agents can complete is growing. These benchmarks establish how well agents perform sustained technical work. OWE-Bench extends this to broader set of artifacts, including CAD, structural and aircraft design, and studies how agents select solutions, assess performance beyond provided cases, and decide when to stop. How agents use their time. Agents do not always use the time they are given. PaperBench found that all models except Claude 3.5 Sonnet frequently finished early, and scaffold that removed the option to stop raised o1s score but lowered Claude 3.5 Sonnets [9]. Each dot represents one models mean score over all tasks and its color runs from grey at 0% to orange at the highest mean (54.6%). Larger dots with bold labels identify the Pareto-efficient models: those for which no alternative achieves at least as high score using fewer tokens (left) or at lower cost (right), and the orange line joins them. Horizontal axes use log scale. Tokens are cumulative input plus output, counting cached input once. Costs are model-usage charges at evaluation-time list prices and exclude hardware, tools and services. plateau unless they track how much of it remains [106]. We vary the time limit itself and find that it can change how much an agent does even when the agent never reaches it, and that models differ in whether it does (Section 7). Engineering artifacts. CAD benchmarks measure reconstruction and program generation from text, drawings or geometry [107, 108, 109, 110], and DesignQA evaluates understanding of engineering requirements [111]. EngDesign, BuildArena and Frontier-Eng evaluate designs through simulation [112, 113, 114]; PLE grades professional deliverables with expert rubrics and constraint checks [115]. Some withhold the final checks. Vibe Building gives the agent development margin check and verifies its building designs against seismic and wind time histories that never enter the loop [116], SimuVerity runs generated Simulink models on withheld scenarios [117], and analog circuit design and heuristic programming benchmarks grade on hidden test benches or private cases while the agent works with its own simulations or public cases [118, 16]. Other benchmarks provide simulation feedback during development: FEACAD and FunCADBench return finite-element or simulation results for agents to revise their designs [10, 11]. CADEngBench instead evaluates single response using parameter perturbations and finite-element analysis [119]. OWE-Bench withholds the final cases in every task, gives the agent the provided cases practitioner would have, and freezes the artifact before grading, which makes the gap between what the agent could check and how the artifact performs on unseen cases measurable. Visible tests, selection and exploits. Hidden final evaluation is established, as in machine learning competitions with private leaderboards [15, 72]. ALE-Bench lets agents score heuristic programs on public cases while working and evaluates the final submission once on private cases [16], and Ahmed et al. [74] study test overfitting on SWE-bench, where patches pass the observed tests but miss cases. Choosing among samples with visible tests or learned verifier is standard in code and math generation [70, 120, 66], though imperfect verifiers limit the gains [75]. Language models stated confidence tracks correctness on short questions but is often too high [121, 122]. Section 6 measures these for long-horizon artifacts: how far development scores and the agents own forecasts overstate hidden performance, how much of the best-of-𝑘 gain they recover, and whether more attempts can replace more time. ImpossibleBench measures propensity to exploit tests on tasks made impossible [81], and Zhu et 34 OWEBench al. [123] set out practices for rigorous agentic benchmarks; Section 8 reports exploit attempts observed during evaluation. Search and information access. Internet-enabled evaluation must account for retrieved solutions and contamination [8, 9, 84, 124]. Fixed corpora and dated snapshots give more controlled retrieval [125, 126, 127, 128], though date bounds do not control ranking signals or model knowledge [97, 129]. WebCode studies search on tasks involving recent library releases [130]; we test whether access to published methods improves performance on engineering tasks that are selected to require substantial adaptation and implementation, measuring both search uptake and final outcomes [131, 132]. Other meanings of open world. The term has established meanings elsewhere: open-set and openworld recognition, in which model must recognize inputs from classes it never saw in training [133, 134]; the open-world assumption in knowledge representation, under which fact missing from database is unknown rather than false [135]; and open-ended environments that keep generating new challenges [136]. We use it in narrower sense: the agent works from what practitioner would have, and judges its work without access to all the conditions that determine its final performance or predefined threshold for completion.
